documents.t: Every application starts the same way: someone hands a developer a requirements document and says 'build this.' The first job as a developer is to turn those definitions into a working database schema.

documents.u: /Procify_Documentation/docs/Docs/Training Guide/Beginner Training Guide/Session 6 — Bindings, Navigation & Styling/G — Implement styling

documents.t: Every control on a Klobase screen reads and writes data through the Transaction Model (\$M). The model is a JSON model object. All bindings use the prefix \$M to reference it. Without a binding, a control shows a static value or nothing at all — it is disconnected from the live data.
documents.s: Part A — Data Bindings In Depth
documents.u: /Procify_Documentation/docs/Docs/Training Guide/Beginner Training Guide/Session 6 — Bindings, Navigation & Styling/Part A — Data Bindings In Depth

documents.t: Expression binding lets you write a JavaScript ternary expression directly inside a binding path string. It starts with \{= and ends with \}. It is evaluated live at runtime whenever the bound model values change.
documents.u: /Procify_Documentation/docs/Docs/Training Guide/Beginner Training Guide/Session 6 — Bindings, Navigation & Styling/Part B — Expression Bindings

documents.t: A formatter function is a TypeScript method in the controller file that takes one or more raw model values as input and returns a formatted display value. It is the right tool whenever expression binding would become too long, needs multi-step logic, or needs to look up external data.
documents.u: /Procify_Documentation/docs/Docs/Training Guide/Beginner Training Guide/Session 6 — Bindings, Navigation & Styling/Part C — Formatter Functions

documents.t: Navigation in Klobase is handled exclusively through the navTo() controller API. All legacy navigation methods (navToS, navToByEvent, navToScreenByKeyScreen) are deprecated — always use navTo. It is defined on KloController and is available in every page controller via this.navTo().

documents.t: The Style Classes tab in the Page Builder is the single place to control all visual formatting. It has two modes a Section, a PageArea/PageLayout, or a Control.

documents.t: Vienable (Visible + Enable) is the declarative system for controlling control visibility and editability across four independent dimensions. The final result for any control is the intersection of all configured dimensions: a control is visible only if ALL applicable dimension rules say it should be visible.

documents.t: Client-side validation in Klobase operates at two levels: (1) field-level required constraints using the 'required' property, and (2) full-form OnValidate triggered by commitP or saveTransaction. Both are enforced in the browser before any network call is made.

documents.t: Before touching any tool, you need a clear picture of the application you are building. Read this section carefully — every configuration decision in Sessions 1– traces back to this Business Requirement Document.
documents.s: Part A — Understanding the Customer complaint Application
documents.u: /Procify_Documentation/docs/Docs/Training Guide/Beginner Training Guide/Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management/Part A — Understanding the Customer complaint Application

documents.t: The Customer Complaints Application is a solution designed to manage customer complaints end-to-end across three personas: • Log and track customer complaints with full lifecycle management. • Route complaints from Employee → Manager → Responsible Team. • Manage complaint line items, voice records, and file attachments. • Monitor escalations, SLA (TAT), and resolution timelines. • Provide dashboards per role so every user sees what they need.
documents.u: /Procify_Documentation/docs/Docs/Training Guide/Beginner Training Guide/Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management/Part A — Understanding the Customer complaint Application

documents.t: This application defines exactly three application roles, each mapped to a Procify role-rollup level for viewable and UI-Auth controls: Role ID Business Name Procify Role Rollup Employee Complaint Creator Owner (s_role_rollup = 10) Manager Complaint Assignor Supervisor (s_role_rollup = 20) Responsible Team Issue Resolver Reviewer (s_role_rollup = 30) 📘 Role Precedence Rule Precedence is a number. Lower = higher priority. Employee: precedence 3, Manager: precedence 2, ResponsibleTeam: precedence 1. This means if a user has multiple roles, the lower-precedence number overrides. Your developer account should be assigned Manager (precedence 2) for full access during testing.

documents.t: The status lifecycle has 6 states. team working on it ON HOLD Purple — Responsible Team placed on hold pending information RESOLVED Green — Responsible Team marked as resolved CLOSED Grey — Manager confirmed resolution and closed the ticket REOPEN Red — Employee or Manager reopened a resolved/closed complaint 📘 Status Transition Rules OPEN → INPROCESS: only Manager can trigger (by assigning responsible_team).INPROCESS → ON HOLD / RESOLVED: only ResponsibleTeam can trigger.RESOLVED → CLOSED: only Manager can trigger.CLOSED → REOPEN: Employee or Manager can reopen; documents.t: Reference: Workspace Hub 7.0 - User Guide Workspace Hub is an Admin Tool that focuses on managing applications and the application users. It is a versatile application that serves diverse purposes from user management to application management. Apart from that, this tool can also be used for modifying the already existing users and apps.
documents.u: /Procify_Documentation/docs/Docs/Training Guide/Beginner Training Guide/Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management/Part B — Workspace Hub Users

documents.t: Workspace Hub menu will be visible for Users who are assigned as TESTER or DEVELOPER or SUPERADMIN for cockpit flavor. Step 1: Go to the menu options and select Workspace Hub. Step 2: The Workspace Hub contains the following Pages.
documents.u: /Procify_Documentation/docs/Docs/Training Guide/Beginner Training Guide/Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management/Part B — Workspace Hub Users

documents.t: A User is a platform-level account — a person who can log in to one or more applications. Users exist independently of applications. You create the person first, then assign them to applications with roles separately. The same user can have different roles in different applications.
documents.u: /Procify_Documentation/docs/Docs/Training Guide/Beginner Training Guide/Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management/Part B — Workspace Hub Users

documents.t: Create one test user to represent the end-user persona (emp01) throughout all sessions. 1 Navigate to Users In the Workspace Hub, click Users in the left navigation. The user list screen loads. 2 Click Create New User Click the create button in the toolbar. 3 Fill in User Details Complete all required fields as shown in the table below. Field What to enter Title Choose the title from dropdown (Mandatory) First Name Fill the first name (Mandatory) Last Name Fill the last name (Optional) Email A real or placeholder email address (Mandatory) Mobile Number used for OTP login if configured (Mandatory) Designation Fill the designation (Mandatory) User ID (Login ID) test_<your_prid> e.g. test_pr0045 BPID Choose bpid from dropdown (Mandatory) Authcode Choose authcode from dropdown (Mandatory) 4 Save the User Click Save. The user is created. Note the User ID — you will reference it when assigning this user to the application. Important — User Created ≠ User Has Access • Creating a user only adds them to the platform's user directory. They cannot access any application until assigned to one with a specific role. You will complete that assignment in Part D of this session. If a user tries to log in before assignment, they will see error mentioning no applications assigned Refer Create User part from workspace hub manual for more information.
documents.u: /Procify_Documentation/docs/Docs/Training Guide/Beginner Training Guide/Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management/Part B — Workspace Hub Users

documents.t: An application is a self-contained unit that holds all the metadata you build — entities, queries, pages, menus, and more. It is the primary organising structure of everything you will do in Sessions 2–8. Users are assigned to applications (with roles), not to individual Pages or features.
documents.s: What Is an Application in Klobase?

The application creation form opens. 3 Fill in Application Details Complete the fields as shown in the table below. Field What to enter App ID Change the App ID according to the application App Name Same as app id Description (optional) Service Request Management training application 4 Save the Application Click Save. The app appears in the Apps list with Active status.
documents.u: /Procify_Documentation/docs/Docs/Training Guide/Beginner Training Guide/Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management/Part C — Workspace Hub Apps & Roles

documents.t: Roles control what a user can do inside the application. Procify has two categories: Role Type What it controls System Roles (built-in) MANAGER,DEVELOPER and TESTER— control access to dev tools (data studio,page builder, Workspace Hub, Private Node). Pre-built into the platform. Application Roles (custom) Roles you define inside your app. Control what users see and can do at runtime within your app's Pages and data. For this training, define single application role inside your app: Role Name Precedence Role Name DeliveryAgent 1 DeliveryAgent Role Precedence — Key Rule • Precedence is a number. Lower number = higher priority. If a user has multiple roles, the one with the lowest precedence number takes effect at runtime. Delivery Admin(1) always overrides Delivery Agent(2) for a user assigned both roles. Your developer account will be Delivery Admin. The test user will be SRM_User. This lets you test both personas.
documents.u: /Procify_Documentation/docs/Docs/Training Guide/Beginner Training Guide/Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management/Part C — Workspace Hub Apps & Roles

documents.t: 1 Open Your Application In the Apps list, click on srm_<prid> to open its detail screen. 2 Go to Roles & Users Click on the Roles & Users tab inside the application detail. 3 Create the DeliveryAgent Role In Application Roles, click Add. Role Name: DeliveryAgent.. Description: Field delivery personnel — can view and manage assigned deliveries. Click Save. 4 Verify Roles Are Listed Delivery Agents appear in the Application Roles list.

documents.s: Assigning the customer complaints to user via employee role
documents.u: /Procify_Documentation/docs/Docs/Training Guide/Beginner Training Guide/Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management/Part D — Workspace Hub App Assignment

documents.t: 1 Open new profile / guest mode Open a new Incognito / Private browser window so it does not use your developer session. 2 Navigate to Your Landscape URL Enter the landscape URL provided by the trainer. 3 Log In as the Test User Use test_<prid> and the password you set. 4 Verify the Application Is Visible The Service Request Management app should appear in the test user's menu. It will be empty — no Pages yet — but its presence confirms the assignment is correct. Troubleshooting — App Not Visible After Assignment • Confirm the user is assigned to the correct role under the correct app. Check that the app is Active in the Workspace Hub. If the test user was already logged in before assignment, log out and log back in. Ensure the test user's account status is Active (not Locked).
documents.u: /Procify_Documentation/docs/Docs/Training Guide/Beginner Training Guide/Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management/Part D — Workspace Hub App Assignment

documents.t: Assigning one test user at a time (as done in Part D) works fine for training, but it does not scale. Real projects onboard users in batches — a new hire cohort, an entire department, or a partner organisation that all needs the same app access on day one. Team Groups (labelled User collections inside the Workspace Hub screen) solve exactly this: they let you bundle a set of users once and assign the whole bundle to an application in a single step, instead of repeating the Part D steps per user. Team Groups are of two kinds: Individual Team Group — created automatically for every user the moment their account is created. Hidden by default (use the Show Individual checkbox to reveal them). Its only job is to let a newly created app be auto-assigned back to the user who created it. Group Team Group — created manually by an admin, and the one you will use for real onboarding work. It holds any number of users and can be linked to one or more App Collections (App Collections) so that every user in the group inherits access to every app in the collection Why Team Groups Matter in Practice Without Team Groups, assigning 25 new employees to 3 apps means 75 manual assignment actions (Part D, repeated). With a Team Group, it becomes: 1 group with 25 members, linked once to an App Collection with 3 apps. Team Groups are filtered by the logged-in user’s Auth Configuration and scoped to the current landscape — you will only see groups you are authorised to manage.
documents.u: /Procify_Documentation/docs/Docs/Training Guide/Beginner Training Guide/Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management/Part D.1 — Team Groups Bulk User Assignment

documents.t: The Customer Complaints BRD defines a ResponsibleTeam persona made up of several support agents, not just one test user. Rather than repeating Part D for each agent individually, model the onboarding the way a real project would: Action Detail / Code Create the Team Group Navigate to Workspace Hub → User Collections (Team Groups). Click Add. Name it grp_response_team_<prid>. Add members Open the group, click Add under members, and select 3–4 existing users (or the test users created earlier in this session) to represent the support agents. Link to an App Collection Under the group’s App Collections tab, add the Customer Complaints App Collection so every member inherits the ResponsibleTeam role assignment. Verify in bulk Log in as any one member. Confirm the app is visible, exactly as verified individually in Part D — but this time achieved through the group, not a per-user step.
documents.u: /Procify_Documentation/docs/Docs/Training Guide/Beginner Training Guide/Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management/Part D.1 — Team Groups Bulk User Assignment

documents.t: For onboarding sets larger than a handful of users, Team Groups also support bulk Excel upload/download, so a spreadsheet of usernames can populate group membership without clicking through the UI one row at a time. This is the same mechanism used for App Collections and is the recommended approach once a group exceeds roughly 10–15 members. 🛠 Hands-On — Try It Yourself Export your grp_response_team_<prid> group to Excel. Add two more (fictional) usernames as new rows. Re-upload the file and confirm the new rows appear as pending/invalid members (since those users don’t yet exist) — this is expected and demonstrates the validation Procify performs on upload.
documents.u: /Procify_Documentation/docs/Docs/Training Guide/Beginner Training Guide/Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management/Part D.1 — Team Groups Bulk User Assignment

documents.t: Every application starts the same way: someone hands a developer a requirements document and says 'build this.' The Customer complaints Application Business Requirement Document (BRD) you read in Session 1 defines exactly what data needs to be stored — 3 data objects, their fields, and their relationships. The first job as a developer is to turn those definitions into a working database schema. Before opening any tool, it is worth understanding what that process looks like — and how much of it Procify eliminates. The rest of this part walks through the traditional process step by step, then shows exactly which steps the data studio replaces.
documents.s: Part E — understanding the importance of Procify
documents.u: /Procify_Documentation/docs/Docs/Training Guide/Beginner Training Guide/Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management/Part E — understanding the importance of Procify

documents.t: 📘 Schema — The Blueprint of Your Application's Data • A schema is the complete definition of the data your application stores: what tables exist, what columns each table has, what type of data each column holds, and how tables relate to each other. The schema is the foundation of every application. Without it, there is no database. Without a database, there is no data. Without data, there is no application. Building the schema is always the first development task after reading a BRD. Everything else — APIs, Pages, logic — is built on top of it. In our BRD, the schema is already defined in Section 4 (Entity Relationship Overview). The 4 entities, their properties, and their relationships are all there. Our job today is to implement that schema.
documents.u: /Procify_Documentation/docs/Docs/Training Guide/Beginner Training Guide/Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management/Part E — understanding the importance of Procify

documents.t: 🏗 How developers build a schema without a low-code platform • Step 1 — Write SQL scripts: A backend developer writes CREATE TABLE statements for each entity. For the Delivery table alone, that is 12 columns — each with its SQL data type, constraints, default values, and indexes. Step 2 — Write an ORM model: For every SQL table, the developer writes a model class in the backend language (Node.js/TypeScript, Python, Java). This class mirrors the database table and handles object-relational mapping. Step 3 — Write REST API endpoints: For each entity, the developer writes GET, POST, PUT, DELETE API handlers. Each handler validates input, maps it to the model, executes the database query, and returns the response. Step 4 — Write validation logic: For each property that has rules (mandatory, unique, min/max), the developer writes validation code — either in the model or in the API handler. Step 5 — Handle database migrations: Every time the schema changes (new property, renamed column), the developer writes a migration script to alter the existing tables without losing data. Step 6 — Test the API: The developer uses Postman or writes unit tests to verify each endpoint returns the correct data in the correct format. Repeat for all 4 entities. 🔴 The pain of the traditional approach • Multiple files across multiple layers — SQL files, model files, API controller files, test files. A change to one field requires edits in 4–6 places. Context switching: a single developer must switch between SQL, backend language, API design, and test writing — each requiring a different mental mode. Time cost: 3–4 days of developer time before a single screen can be shown to a stakeholder. Repetition: most of this work is identical boilerplate — every entity needs the same pattern of SQL + ORM + CRUD APIs. Nothing creative, just repetitive.
documents.s: The Traditional Way of Building a Schema
documents.u: /Procify_Documentation/docs/Docs/Training Guide/Beginner Training Guide/Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management/Part E — understanding the importance of Procify

documents.t: ✅ How Procifyreplaces the traditional schema-building process • In Klobase, all 6 traditional steps are replaced by a single tool: the data studio. You define the entity (name, type) → add properties (name, data type, key attributes) → click Update Schema. Done. The platform automatically generates: the database table (SQL step 1), the data access layer (ORM step 2), the REST API endpoints (step 3), basic validation from key attributes (step 4), and handles schema updates automatically (step 5). There are no separate files to keep in sync. The data studio is the single source of truth. Everything downstream — API, data validation, mobile sync — is derived from it automatically. Time with Klobase: the same 4 entities, all properties, schema live in the database — approximately 2 hours in this session. The developer's time is freed for the parts that actually require thinking: business logic, UI design, user experience. This is not an approximation. Let us make it concrete: Traditional Task data studio Replacement Write CREATE TABLE SQL for Delivery entity Create entity in data studio — choose type, add properties, click Save Write ORM model class (12 fields × 4 entities) Already done — properties ARE the model Write 16+ REST API endpoints Already done — fireQuery apis are available to fetch data Write validation for mandatory fields Check the Mandatory key attribute icon on the property and validation will be handled by platform. Write database migration script Click Update Schema again — the platform handles ALTER TABLE automatically Test APIs with Postman Use the built-in Test function in the data studio toolbar
documents.u: /Procify_Documentation/docs/Docs/Training Guide/Beginner Training Guide/Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management/Part E — understanding the importance of Procify

documents.t: 🔴 Traditional screen development requires five separate layers • 1. HTML / JSX template — the visual structure: list container, card component, placeholder slots for each field. 2. CSS / styling — card appearance, status badge colours, spacing, responsiveness for mobile and desktop. 3. API call — GET /complaints?user={currentUser.id} to fetch complaint records from the server. 4. State management (React state, Redux, etc.) — store the fetched array, handle loading state, handle error state, trigger re-renders when data changes. 5. Data binding — map each complaint object's fields to the template slots: {complaint.complaint_desc}, {complaint.priority}. Total: 3–5 files, 150–300 lines of code, for one list screen. Any change to one layer often requires changes to the others.
documents.s: The Traditional Way of Building a UI
documents.u: /Procify_Documentation/docs/Docs/Training Guide/Beginner Training Guide/Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management/Part E — understanding the importance of Procify

documents.t: ✅ The Page Builder replaces all five layers with a single metadata configuration • In the Page Builder you configure the screen structure. The platform reads your configuration and generates the visual rendering, handles all data fetching, manages state automatically, applies your styling choices, and wires up the data bindings. This means: one tool, no files to keep in sync, no merge conflicts on screen structure, no state management code. The Page Wizard (used in this session) gives you a ready-made screen in minutes. Session 2 teaches you to build the same screen step-by-step so you understand every level of the hierarchy. Pages configured in the Page Builder render identically on both browser (web) and mobile (KloTouch) — no separate mobile codebase needed.
documents.s: The Procify Way — The Page Wizard & Page Builder
documents.u: /Procify_Documentation/docs/Docs/Training Guide/Beginner Training Guide/Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management/Part E — understanding the importance of Procify

documents.t: Now that you understand what Procify eliminates, you will experience it firsthand. You will create the d_complaints entity and its Complaints list screen — using the Page Wizard — in this session. Session 2 will rebuild the same screen step-by-step so you understand every level of the hierarchy.

documents.t: ⚠ Naming rules — read before creating anything Only lowercase letters, numbers, and underscores. No spaces, hyphens, or capitals. IDs cannot be changed after creation — a wrong name requires deleting and recreating. Never use "user" as an entity ID — reserved keyword in MySQL. d_ prefix = Runtime Entity — always use this prefix for transactional entities. 1 Click the + button in the tree → select Entity. The entity creation dialog opens. 2 Entity ID: d_complaints. Click Create. 3 When prompted for the Primary Key — Property ID: complaint_id | Kind: Primary | Data Type: Auto Number. Click Submit. 4 Click Save. d_complaints appear in the left tree.
documents.u: /Procify_Documentation/docs/Docs/Training Guide/Beginner Training Guide/Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management/Part F — Creating the d_complaints Entity and Initial Page Using the Wizard

documents.t: Follow the steps below to add each property. The complete property reference table is in Part A. 1 Click on d_complaints in the tree to select it. 2 Click on the Properties tab in the detail panel. 3 Click the + button to add a new property. The qualifier selection menu opens. 4 Select the qualifier (Regular for most properties) → fill in Property ID, Data Type, and Short Label. 5 Toggle key attributes where required: ❗ Mandatory for complaint_desc. 6 Click Save after each batch of properties. 7 Repeat for all 20 properties listed in the d_complaints table in Part A. ⚠ Data type reminder Use Text (not String) for complaint_desc and remark — they exceed 255 characters. Use Timestamp for all date fields: first_response_date, planned_resolution_date, closed_on, created_on, modified_on. Use Boolean for is_escalated — not String. Use Decimal for actual_tat and standard_tat.

documents.t: The Page Wizard creates a full working screen — with page, layout, area, section, and controls — in a few clicks. Use it now to produce your first Complaints screen quickly. In Session 2 you will build the same screen manually, step-by-step, so you understand every level. 1 From the main menu, open Page Builder (under Design Studio). 2 In the application dropdown, select customer_complaints_<prid>. 3 Click the Edit icon → click the + icon → select Create Page from Wizard. 4 Page ID: p_complaints | Title: Complaints | Lead Entity: d_complaints. Click Generate. 8 The wizard creates the full page hierarchy automatically. Click Save. 9 Click Show Full Preview to verify the three test complaint records appear as cards in the list. 📘 What the wizard created Page: p_complaints (with route /complaints) Page Layout: pl_complaints_desk (Stack type) Page Area: pa_complaints (assigned to the layout) Section: s_complaint_search (Search type — for filtering) Section: s_complaint_list (CardList type — shows all complaints) Section: s_complaint_detail (Form type — shows one selected complaint) All controls bound to the correct d_complaints properties automatically. In Session 2 you will understand every one of these elements and rebuild it from scratch.

documents.t: A Business Object is a hierarchical tree of entities. The root entity represents the BO. Child entities are dependent on the root via Primary Relations. Standalone entities are linked via Non-Primary (Aggregated) Relations. 📘 BO Hierarchy — Customer Complaints d_complaints (Root Entity / BO) d_complaint_item (Root Entity / BO) d_complaint_voices (Root Entity / BO) d_complaints_attachment (Root Entity / BO) d_customers (Root Entity / BO) d_resp_team (Root Entity / BO)

documents.t: Before building screens, every developer must be familiar with the two core design tools in Klobase: the Data Studio (Procify Data Studio) and the Page Builder (Procify Page Builder). This part gives you an orientation of both tools and their layouts, then walks through building the Customer Complaints screen step by step — showing the expected output at each stage.
documents.s: Part B — Understanding Data Studio and Page Builder
documents.u: /Procify_Documentation/docs/Docs/Training Guide/Beginner Training Guide/Session 2 — BOL Entity Fundamentals & Initial Pages/Part B — Understanding Data Studio and Page Builder

documents.t: Navigate to Design Studio → Data Studio. The editor is divided into two major sections: the Tree on the left and the Detail on the right. Section What It Does Tree (Left) Lists all entities, queries, and value helps in the selected app. Click any item to load it in the Detail panel. Use Expand All / Collapse All to navigate. Use the search bar to find entities quickly. Detail (Right) Shows all configuration tabs for the selected object: Properties, Relations, Object Type, Status, Queries, Rules, Entity Index. Only visible when an item is selected from the tree. Toolbar (Top) Context-sensitive: Save, Edit, Update Schema, Validate, Delete, Test, Metadata File. Actions change depending on what is selected in the tree. App Selector Dropdown at the top-left to switch between your assigned apps. Always verify the correct app is selected before making any changes. Normal / Expert Mode Toggle in the toolbar. Normal Mode: Entity, Query, Value Help creation. Expert Mode: adds Status Config, Object Group Config, Entity Index. Expert Mode needed from Session 3 onwards. Note: Currently there is no difference between expert mode and normal mode 📘 Data Studio Reference Source: Procify Data Studio 7.0 User Guide — Sections 2.0 Editor Sections, 1.4 Modes Tree: expand, collapse, filter — same panel used for all entity operations. Detail panel tabs depend on context: entity selected shows Properties/Relations/Status; query shows query config. Update Schema: converts entity metadata into actual DB table. Required after every property change. Test button: opens the Data Browser for CRUD operations on the entity directly from the editor.
documents.s: B.1 — Data Studio (Procify Data Studio) — Tool Layout
documents.u: /Procify_Documentation/docs/Docs/Training Guide/Beginner Training Guide/Session 2 — BOL Entity Fundamentals & Initial Pages/Part B — Understanding Data Studio and Page Builder

documents.t: Navigate to Design Studio → Page Builder. According to the Procify Page Builder 7.0 User Guide, the editor is divided into four major sections: Section What It Does Tree (Left) Hierarchical view of the entire page structure: Page → Page Layout → Page Area → Section → Controls. All creation, renaming, and assignment is done via right-click context menu in this tree. Preview (Centre) Live render of the screen. Refreshes on Save. Use the Auto Refresh toggle for real-time updates. Full Preview loads actual data from the database for testing. Detail (Down) Configuration panel for the selected tree element. Shows different properties depending on whether you have selected a Page, Page Layout, Page Area, Section, or Control. Page Data Model (Right — Tab) TransNode configuration. Defines what data is available to the page. Use the + button to add Model Paths. Each TransNode has: an ID, an Entity/Query binding, a Node Type (EntitySet / Entity / Query), and an optional Fold From parent. 📘 Page Builder Toolbar Reference (Procify Page Builder 7.0 User Guide — Section 1.0) Edit icon — enables edit mode on the tree. You MUST click this before creating or renaming anything. + icon — create a new page (blank or from wizard). Save icon — commits all pending changes. Required before preview refreshes. Show Full Preview — loads real database records into the preview for testing. Detail icon — toggles visibility of the detail properties panel. Page Data Model icon — toggles visibility of the TransNode / data model panel. Reset Perspective — restores all panels to their default size and position. Preview In — switch preview between desktop, tablet, and mobile device views.
documents.s: B.2 — Page Builder (Procify Page Builder) — Tool Layout
documents.u: /Procify_Documentation/docs/Docs/Training Guide/Beginner Training Guide/Session 2 — BOL Entity Fundamentals & Initial Pages/Part B — Understanding Data Studio and Page Builder

documents.t: Every screen in Klobase follows a strict 5-level hierarchy. This is the most important structural concept in UI development. Each level has a mandatory naming convention prefix: 📘 Five-Level Page Hierarchy Level 1 — PAGE (prefix: p_) The root container. Holds all layouts. Created first. One page can have multiple layouts (one per device type). At runtime, the platform picks the layout based on device: screencontainerdesktop, screencontainermobile, screencontainertab, screencontainerdefault. Level 2 — PAGE LAYOUT (prefix: pl_) Sits directly under the Page. Defines HOW the page areas are arranged. screenType options: stack, tab, two_column, object_page, grid_layout, hsplitter, vsplitter. Example: pl_complaints_desk (two column layout for desktop). Level 3 — PAGE AREA (prefix: pa_) A logical sub-container inside the layout. Can itself have a screenType (tab, stack, splitter). Sections are assigned to page areas to determine WHERE they render. Example: pa_complaints (list area), pa_complaint_details (detail area). Level 4 — SECTION (prefix: s_) The rendering unit. screenType determines HOW it displays data. Types: search, cardlist, card, form, grid, tree, timeline, map, calendar. Must be assigned to a Page Area to appear in the UI. Example: s_search (search), s_complaints (grid), s_detail_header (form). Level 5 — CONTROLS Individual fields, buttons, labels, icons bound to entity properties. Added via: right-click section → New → Controls, OR drag from unused TransNode properties. Section screenType Renders As search Filter bar with Close / Reset / Search buttons. Auto-generates the search toolbar. cardlist List of records as card rows — one card per record. Good for mobile and compact lists. grid Tabular list with column headers and rows. Supports sort, filter, group-by per column. form Detail form layout. Each control renders as a labelled input field. card Single entity rendered as a CSS grid card. One record only. tab Used on Page Areas to group child sections as tabs. showTitle must be true for tab labels. tree Hierarchical tree display for nested data.
documents.s: B.3 — The Page Hierarchy (Procify Page Builder 7.0 User Guide — Sections 3.0–7.0)
documents.u: /Procify_Documentation/docs/Docs/Training Guide/Beginner Training Guide/Session 2 — BOL Entity Fundamentals & Initial Pages/Part B — Understanding Data Studio and Page Builder

documents.t: The Page Data Model defines the data available to a screen. Every section and control that displays data must be bound to a TransNode. A TransNode is a “data pipe” — it fetches entity records from the database and makes them available to sections and controls on the page. Node Type Fetches EntitySet A LIST of records. Use for search sections, grids, card lists. Suffix convention: _list. Example: d_complaints_list Entity ONE record (the currently selected record). Use for detail forms. Suffix convention: _detail. Example: d_complaints_detail Query Records from a kloQuery with WHERE conditions, joins, sorting. Suffix convention: _query. Other Non-standard / custom use cases. 📘 Fold From — The Critical Link Between List and Detail When you create d_complaints_detail (Entity type) and set its “Fold From” = d_complaints_list, the platform automatically loads the selected record’s data into d_complaints_detail whenever the user clicks a row in the list. This is the mechanism that connects list → detail. Without Fold From: the detail section will always be empty. With Fold From: clicking any complaint row in the list instantly populates the detail form. TransNode naming convention (from Procify Page Builder 7.0 Guide): EntitySet → _list suffix Entity → _detail suffix Query → _query suffix
documents.u: /Procify_Documentation/docs/Docs/Training Guide/Beginner Training Guide/Session 2 — BOL Entity Fundamentals & Initial Pages/Part B — Understanding Data Studio and Page Builder

documents.t: Based on the Customer Complaints Application design, the p_complaints page has two page areas. The complete target structure is: 📘 p_complaints — Full Page Structure PAGE: p_complaints └─ pl_complaints_desk (PageLayout — screenType: two column) ├─ pa_complaints (PageArea 1 — List Panel) | ├─ s_search (Section — screenType: search) | | Controls: ticket_id, desc, customer_id, responsible_tea, priority, | | s_status, is_escalated, cust_category, cust_type, | | complaint_type, raised_by, state, nature_of_compl, actual_tat, standard_tat | └─ s_complaints (Section — screenType: grid) | Controls: ticket_id (link), customer_id, priority, s_status, | planned_res_dat, closed_on, sales_manager └─ pa_complaint_details (PageArea 2 — Tab) ├─ section_toolbar (Action toolbar: Edit/Save/Add buttons) ├─ s_detail_header (Section — screenType: card— key fields) | Controls: desc, i_ageing, t_ageing, s_status, i_t_priority, i_res_team, responsible_tea └─ pa_comp_details (PageArea — screenType: default) ├─ s_complaint_details ├─ s_complaint_details3 → form ├─ s_complaint_details5 ├─ s_reporter_details —> form ├─ s_complaint_details2 ├─ s_complaint_details4 → form

documents.t: 1 Open Page Builder from Design Studio → Page Builder. Select your application from the app dropdown. 2 Click the Edit icon in the toolbar to enable edit mode. 3 Click the + icon → Create Blank Page. 4 Page ID: p_complaints | Title: Employee Complaints | Lead Entity: d_complaints(use vh). Click Create. 5 The page appears in the tree. No layouts yet — proceed to Step 2.

documents.t: The Page Layout sits directly under the Page and defines the arrangement type for all page areas. According to Procify Page Builder 7.0 Guide (Section 4.0): at runtime only one pageLayout is picked based on the device type — determined by the page’s screencontainerdefault, screencontainerdesktop, etc. properties. 1 In the tree, right-click on p_complaints → New → Page Layout. A new layout is added to the tree. 2 Right-click the new layout → Rename → enter: pl_complaints_desk. Press Enter. 3 Click pl_complaints_desk in the tree to open its Detail panel on the right. 4 In the Detail panel, set screenType = two column. This renders all assigned page areas one after another — the standard layout for list+detail screens. 5 Now click on p_complaints in the tree. In its Detail panel, set screencontainerdefault = pl_complaints_desk. This tells the platform: use this layout on all devices unless a device-specific layout is set. 6 Save. 📘 Layout Type Quick Reference (Procify Page Builder 7.0 Guide — Section 12.0) stack — Sections / areas render one after another vertically. One subscreen shown at a time. two_column — Master-detail split: left panel (list) + right panel (detail). Max 2 columns. tab — Renders children as tabbed panels. Used at Page Area level for detail tabs. object_page — SAP-style object page: sticky header + tab body sections. hsplitter — Horizontal split with resizable rows. vsplitter — Vertical split with resizable columns. grid_layout / css_grid — CSS Grid-based placement. Requires modeller configuration.

Dialog opens. 2 Node Path : search | Entity/Query: d_complaints | Node Type: Query. Click OK. 3 Click Transfer&Link of search. Node Path: list 4 Click Transfer&Link of list Node Path: detail 5 Save. These two TransNodes are the data backbone for all sections on this page.

documents.t: Per Procify Page Builder 7.0 Guide (Section 6.1): To add a new section, right-click on the page area and select New → Section. The search screenType auto-generates the filter bar with Close / Reset / Search buttons. 1 Right-click on pa_complaints → New → Section. Rename it: s_search. 2 In the Detail panel, set screenType = search. 4 Select s_search in the tree. In the Detail panel, set the TransNode (path) = search. 5 Add controls: right-click s_search →click New in poup → Controls . OR go to the Page Data Model panel → select search→ Unused Properties tab → drag properties directly to s_search in the tree. 6 Add all controls as listed in the note below. Save after each set. 📘 s_search Controls — Match the Search Bar in the Screenshot Row 1: complaint_id (Ticket Id text input), s_status, complaint_type Row 2: desc (Description text input), is_escalated (Escalated checkbox), nature_of_compl Row 3: customer_id (Employee ID — with Value Help picker icon), cust_category (Employee, actual_tat (Actual TAT number input) Row 4: priority, cust_type , standard_tat (Standard TAT number input) Tree also shows: raised_by, state, cust_category_lbl, cust_type_lbl (label controls for display) How to add controls via drag-and-drop (Procify Page Builder 7.0 Guide — Section 2.2.6 DnD on Preview): 1. In the Page Data Model panel, select search→ click Unused Properties tab. 2. Drag any property from the unused list and drop it onto s_search in the tree. 3. The control is created automatically with the property binding pre-set. 4. You can drag and drop controls within the section to align the controls. 📸 Final Output — After Creating s_search Once s_search is created with all controls and you click Show Full Preview, you will see the search filter bar rendered at the top of the screen exactly as shown below. Expected output: s_search renders the Employee Complaints filter bar with all fields — Ticket Id, Status, Complaint Type, Escalated checkbox, Employee Category, Priority, Nature of Complaint, Actual TAT, and Standard TAT. Close / Reset / Search buttons are auto-generated by the search scr eenType. 📸 Tree View — How s_search Looks in the Page Builder Tree After adding all controls, s_search in the tree should look like the screenshot below. Each control is listed under the section with its entity property binding. documents.t: The grid section renders complaint records as rows with sortable, filterable columns. Per Procify Page Builder 7.0 Guide (Section 6.2 — Grid): For desktop view, section screenType should be “grid”. Add a conf_grid000 config node for grid behaviour settings. 1 Right-click pa_complaints → New → Section. Rename: s_complaints. 2 In the Detail panel, set screenType = grid. 3 Set TransNode path = list. 4 Right-click pa_complaints → New → Assign → select s_complaints (below s_search). Save. 5 Add controls from d_complaints_list TransNode unused properties: ticket_id (set the control type as m.link and add press event with function as ‘navTo’(Fill the sunscreen id as detail page area) ), customer_id, priority, s_status, planned_res_dat, closed_on, sales_manager. 6 Right-click s_complaints → New → Config → rename: conf_grid000. This config node stores grid behaviour properties. 7 Right-click s_complaints → New → Toolbar. Add Add and Delete buttons in the toolbar detail. 8 Arrange the controls in s_complaints by using drag and drop feature inside section 9 Save. 📸 Final Output — After Creating s_complaint Once s_complaints is created with all controls and you click Show Full Preview, you will see the complaints list rendered below search section You can notice that the screen we created is not the same in the provided screenshot. Complaint_id contains id-desc Status has color Grid is occupying full screen Pont 1 & 2 will be achieved in the upcoming sessions. For point 3 we can achieve this by setting screentype of pa_complaints as fit_to_area and mark auto_height as true for s_complaints layout. 📸 Tree View — How s_complaints Looks in the Page Builder Tree After building s_complaints, it should appear in the tree as shown below — with ticket_id as a navigation link, all property controls, conf_grid000, and section_toolbar. Page Builder tree showing s_complaints with controls: ticket_id (link icon), customer_id, priority, s_status, planned_res_dat, closed_on, sales_manager, plus conf_grid000 config and section_toolbar

documents.t: An Entity Relation tells the Klobase server how two entities are connected to each other. Without a relation defined in the Procify Data Studio, the platform has no way to automatically load child records when a parent record is selected — and no way to bundle the BO for save/delete operations. There are two types of relations in Klobase: Relation Type What It Means Primary Relation Tight parent-child bond WITHIN the same Business Object (BO). A child entity is dependent on the parent. Prefixed pr_. Used for d_complaint_item, d_complaint_voices, d_complaints_attachment — all children of d_complaints. Non-Primary (Aggregated) Relation Looser link BETWEEN BOs. Used to reference standalone master entities. Prefixed r_. Used for d_customers and d_resp_team which are independent master entities. 📘 Why Relations Matter in the UI When a relation is defined and referenced in a TransNode in the Page Builder, the platform automatically fetches the child/linked entity records when the parent record is loaded. Without a relation, you would have to write manual queries and wire up the data fetch yourself. The TransNode type 'Relation' in the Page Data Model uses the relation name defined here — this is why naming the relation correctly matters. Naming convention (from Procify Data Studio 7.0 User Guide — Best Practices): pr_ prefix for primary relations, r_ prefix for associated/aggregated relations. Always lowercase.

Follow these steps for r_customer # Action Detail 1 d_complaints Relations tab click d_complaints in the tree and go back to the Relations tab. 2 Click Add Click the Add (+) icon to add a new relation row. 3 Fill Relation Details Relation Name: r_customer | Description: Aggregated relation — customer master data | Return Entity: d_customers | Relation Query: d_customers | Cardinality: 1:1 4 Configure Mapping Click Mapping. Add: Source Property = customer_id | Mapping Type = ON QUERY | Target Property = customer_id. This join fetches d_customers data when a complaint is loaded. 5 Save Click Save. 💡 Mapping Type — BOTH Explained ON CREATE: When a new d_complaint_item is created under a d_complaints parent, the platform automatically copies the complaint_id value into the ticket_id field of the new item. You never have to set this manually. ON QUERY: When you query d_complaint_item records for a given complaint, the platform uses ticket_id = complaint_id as the WHERE condition automatically. BOTH: Use this for standard parent-child relations — it handles both the create and the fetch scenarios. documents.t: In Klobase, an Object Type (stored in the system property s_object_type) is a classification that tags each record as belonging to a specific type. Object Types serve two important purposes: They enable role-based visibility: a button or field can be made visible/editable only for a specific role AND a specific object type combination. This is used for screen behavior in Session 7. They allow ID Series to be object-type-specific: a different number series prefix can be applied per object type — for example, complaints created by Maventic employees might use a different prefix than those created by Procify employees. 📘 Object Type vs Object Group Object Group is a container that groups related Object Types together. The group is used as the filter boundary. Object Type is the actual tag applied to individual records (e.g. MAVENTIC, PROCIFY). Every Object Type must belong to exactly one Object Group. For the Customer Complaints application: • Object Group = company_types Object Types = MAVENTIC, PROCIFY Best Practice (Procify Data Studio 7.0 User Guide): Always maintain an Object Group to group types — the same group can be used in default filters based on users.

documents.t: The system property s_status represents the current state of a complaint record. The Status tab in the Data Studio lets you define the allowed values for s_status and group them into Status Groups. Status Groups are named collections of statuses. They are used in Vienable (Session 7) to control screen behaviour: for example, the Edit button is visible only when s_status is in the OPEN_GROUP, and the Assign Team button is visible only when s_status is in the INPROCESS_GROUP. 📘 Status Lifecycle for Customer Complaints The complaint lifecycle defined in the BRD has 6 states: OPEN → INPROCESS → ON_HOLD / RESOLVED → CLOSED / REOPEN Each status transition is triggered by a specific role (defined in the Role Responsibility matrix from Session 1 Part A). In this session you define the status values and groups. The actual UI enforcement of transitions using Vienable happens in Session 7.

documents.t: An ID Series is a platform-managed counter that automatically generates primary key values when a new record is created. Without an ID Series on complaint_id, a developer would need to generate unique IDs manually — which is error-prone and cannot produce readable, formatted numbers like CMP-00001. ID Series Type Description Auto Number Returns an incrementing number. Combined with a Prefix pattern to produce CMP-00001, CMP-00002, etc. GUID Returns a 32-character UUID. Good for distributed offline scenarios. Not human-readable. None No auto-generation. The developer or rule must set the key manually.

documents.t: # Action Detail 1 Select d_complaints In the Data Studio tree, click on d_complaints. 2 Go to Properties tab Click the Properties tab in the Detail panel. Locate the complaint_id property row. 3 Open ID Series Click the navigation right arrow (→) at the end of the complaint_id row. The ID Series dialog opens for this property. 4 Click Add Click the Add (+) icon in the ID Series dialog. A new entry row appears. 5 Fill ID Series details ID: idp_complaint | Type: Auto Number | From: 1 | Prefix: P- | Chunk Size: 100 | Increment: 1 | Scope: Global | Description: Auto-number for complaint IDs with P- prefix. 6 Click Add Click the Add (+) icon in the ID Series dialog. A new entry row appears. 7 Fill ID Series details ID: idm_complaint | Type: Auto Number | From: 1 | Prefix: M- | Chunk Size: 100 | Increment: 1 | Scope: Global | Description: Auto-number for complaint IDs with P- prefix. 8 Close dialog Click Close on the dialog. The ID Series entry is saved. 9 Save Click Save in the Data Studio toolbar. The complaint_id property now has an ID Series configured. 📘 ID Series Fields Reference (Procify Data Studio 7.0 User Guide — Section 3.0.1 Creating ID Series) ID: Unique ID of the series. Naming convention: id_ prefix, all lowercase. Example: id_complaint. Type: Auto Number = incremental counter. Most common for business records. From: Starting number for the series. Use 1 to start from P-00001. Prefix: Text prepended before the number. P- produces P-1, P-2, etc. Chunk Size: Default 100. The server pre-allocates this many IDs per session (important for offline apps). Scope: Global (default) — one counter shared across all users and tenants. Pattern: Can be used to produce complex formats. For simple prefix + number, just use the Prefix field.

documents.t: By the end of this session, you will be able to: Understand what Entity Relations are and create Primary and Non-Primary (Aggregated) relations between entities. Understand what Object Types are, why they are needed, and configure complaint type classifications for d_complaints. Configure Status and Status Groups to represent the complaint lifecycle (OPEN → INPROCESS → ON HOLD → RESOLVED → CLOSED → REOPEN). Set up an ID Series for complaint_id to auto-generate readable complaint numbers (e.g. CMP-00001). Update the p_complaints UI to reflect the new entity configuration — making the complaint_type, status, and complaint_id fields work correctly in the page. 📘 What This Session Builds On Session 1 created the application, roles, users, and d_complaints entity with raw properties. Session 2 created the remaining 5 entities and built the full p_complaints page step by step. Session 3 enriches the d_complaints entity with the platform features that turn raw fields into intelligent, lifecycle-aware data. After Session 3, the complaint_id will auto-generate, the status dropdown will show the correct lifecycle values, and complaint_type will be classified.

documents.t: A Value Help (VH) is a platform-level component that provides a controlled list of choices for an entity property. When a VH is assigned to a property, the corresponding input field in the UI automatically renders as a dropdown (ComboBox), auto-complete field, or picker dialog (F4) — without any additional coding. The VH also validates that the entered value exists in the list when 'Is Restricted' is enabled. 📘 Three VH Types in Klobase (VH User Guide — Section 1.1) VH Config: Values are maintained in the metadata (config) DB. App-managed, flavor-dependent. Can be overridden by child apps. Requires a build after creation/update. Use for fixed classification lists (priority, complaint_type, etc.). VH Query: Values are fetched from a transactional or modelled query at runtime. Use for dynamic master data pickers (customer_id, responsible_team). The query determines what data appears in the picker. VH Transaction (DEPRECATED): Older type. Internally still supported for legacy apps. New development should use VH Config or VH Query instead. VH Type Source Naming Use Case for This App VH Config Metadata / Config DB vhc_<name> priority, complaint_type, nature_of_complaint VH Query Transactional / Modelled Query vhq_<name> customer_id → d_customers, responsible_team → d_resp_team

documents.t: VH Config stores its values in the metadata database — the same database that stores entity definitions, page structures, and app metadata. These values are part of the application definition itself, not the transaction data. Use VH Config for lists that are defined once by the developer and rarely change: priority levels, complaint categories, nature classifications.

documents.t: A VH Query fetches its suggestion items from a live entity or modelled query at runtime. Unlike VH Config (which is static metadata), VH Query shows records that are currently in the transactional database. This is the right choice for master entity pickers — where the data comes from d_customers, d_resp_team, or any other entity that can be searched and selected. 📘 VH Query Fields (Procify Data Studio 7.0 User Guide — Section 2.2.3 Value Help Detail) Entity/Query: The entity name or modelled query ID that returns the list of suggestions. Key Property: The property whose value gets STORED in the parent entity when the user selects an item. For d_customers → customer_id. Display Text: The property shown to the user in the dropdown/picker. For d_customers → customer_name. Desc Format: How the display appears. Example: :customer_id--:customer_name shows ID followed by Name. Icon: Optional — entity property that holds an icon URL to show alongside each suggestion item.

Click Create. 2 Open vhq_customer Click vhq_customer in the tree. The Detail panel shows the VH Query configuration fields. 3 Set Entity/Query In the Entity/Query field, select d_customers. This means the VH will execute a runtime query against d_customers to fetch suggestion rows. 4 Set Key Property Key Property: customer_id. This is the value that gets written into d_complaints.customer_id when the user picks a customer. 5 Set Display Text Display Text: customer_name. This is what the user sees in the dropdown list. 6 Set Desc Format Desc Format: :customer_id--:customer_name. This renders as 'CUST-001 -- Acme Corp' in the picker field once a value is selected. 7 Save Click Save. vhq_customer is ready. Perform the same for vhq_res_team

Select vhq_resp_team. 4 Save Click Save. 💡 VH Type in the UI Control (KloControls 7.0 User Guide — KloInput) After assigning a VH to a property, the KloInput control in the UI renders differently based on the vhType setting in the Page Data Model or the control's properties panel. F4: Shows a full picker dialog when the user clicks the input — best for large datasets (d_customers with many records). ComboBox: Shows a dropdown list — best for small fixed lists (priority, complaint_type). AutoComplete: Shows suggestions as the user types — best for name-search scenarios. The platform automatically uses the appropriate type based on the VH type. You can override it in the Page Data Model or the control properties.

documents.t: A KloQuery is the Klobase equivalent of a SQL SELECT statement. It lets you define — within the Data Studio — exactly what records to fetch, from which entity, with which filters, joins, and sort order. Unlike a Runtime Entity Query (which simply fetches all records of an entity), a Modelled Query gives you full control over the WHERE clause, JOIN entities, and sort order — and is reusable across multiple pages. Query Type When to Use Runtime Query (Entity Query) Fetch all records of a single entity. No WHERE clause in the definition. Filters applied at runtime via the TransNode. Use for simple list screens. Modelled Query (Dynamic Query) Define custom WHERE conditions, joins, sort order in the Procify Data Studio. Reusable, entity-independent. Use for role-filtered lists (My Complaints), VH Queries backed by joins, aggregated results. Native Query (Advanced Query) Raw SQL. Database-specific. Use only for special cases not achievable with modelled queries. Avoid training. 📘 KloQuery Fields Reference (Procify Data Studio 7.0 User Guide — Section 3.0.2) Return Entity: The entity whose properties appear in the result set. Query Type: Runtime | Modelled | Native — affects which tabs are available. Entities And Join: Add the root entity and any joined entities (LEFT JOIN, INNER JOIN, etc.). Select Properties: Choose which properties from the entities appear in the result. Parameters: Define input parameters the query accepts at runtime (e.g., user_id filter passed from the TransNode). Where: Define filter conditions: entity.property = :parameter or entity.property = 'fixed_value'. Sort Order: Set the default sorting column and direction (ASC / DESC). Naming convention: Query IDs must start with q_. All lowercase.

documents.t: A Saved Query is a named combination of a base query and a specific set of pre-filled search parameters. Where a Modelled Query defines the structure, a Saved Query defines a pre-configured instance of that query — ready to execute with one click in the search bar. Saved Queries appear as quick-filter options in the search TransNode of the UI. 📘 Saved Query vs Modelled Query (Basic Training Guide — Section 2.1) Modelled Query: The definition — entity, properties, parameters, WHERE logic. Reusable structure. Saved Query: A named configuration of a modelled query with preset parameter values. Stored per entity. In the UI, a Saved Query appears as a quick-filter button or dropdown in the search bar section. Saved Queries are created from the Data Browser (Advanced Search), not directly in the query detail tab. Naming convention for Saved Query IDs: Begin with sq_ by convention.

documents.t: # Action Detail 1 Open Data Browser Select d_complaints in the Data Studio tree. Click the data browser in the toolbar. The Data Browser opens. 2 Open Advanced Search In the Data Browser toolbar, click the Advance Search button. A search configuration dialog opens. 3 Select Base Query In the Query field of the Advance click + 4 Set parameter values Select customer_id in the left input and like in the middle input. Enter: $SYSTEM.userID as the parameter value. This means the saved query will always use the logged-in user's ID at runtime. 5 Save as Saved Query Click the Save Query button (or the Save icon in the Advance Search toolbar). Enter Saved Query ID: sq_my_complaints | Description: My Complaints — filter by current user. Click Save. 6 Verify Click search. The Data Browser should show only complaints where assigned_to matches the current user (or empty if no matches). The saved query is now available.

documents.t: 📘 Session 5: BOL Logic & Validations With VH and Queries in place, Session 5 introduces server-side business logic via the Private Node TypeScript environment. Entity Lifecycle Hooks: onCreate, onValidate, onAfterSave, onDelete callbacks in the entity .ts file. Validations: Mandatory field checks, custom error messages, business rule enforcement (e.g. planned_resolution_date must be after created_on). Role-based logic: Using hasPermission() and hasCRUDPermission() to enforce who can transition complaint status. Setting default values: Auto-setting s_status = 'OPEN' on complaint creation, auto-populating created_by from $SYSTEM.userID. Query Rules: beforeQ/afterQ callbacks on the query file — role-based row filtering and post-fetch computed fields.

documents.t: By the end of this session, you will be able to: Understand the three types of Value Helps (VH Config, VH Query, VH Transaction) and when to use each. Create a VH Config for priority (Low / Medium / High / Critical) and nature_of_complaint, complaint_type fields. Create VH Query types that fetch data from d_customers and d_resp_team entities as picker suggestions. Understand what a KloQuery is and how it differs from a Runtime Entity query. Create two Saved Queries for the complaint list: My Complaints (filtered by assigned_to = current user) and All Open Complaints (filtered by s_status = OPEN). Assign Value Helps to entity properties in the Procify Data Studio. Update the UI — wire VH pickers and query-driven TransNodes into the p_complaints search and detail sections. 📘 What This Session Builds On Session 3 configured Relations, Object Types, Status, and ID Series on d_complaints — the structural foundation. Session 4 makes the user experience intelligent: instead of typing raw IDs, users get dropdowns and pickers. priority, complaint_type, nature_of_complaint → VH Config (fixed, app-managed lists). customer_id, responsible_team → VH Query (dynamic, fetched from d_customers / d_resp_team). Saved Queries → drive the different list views per role (My Complaints for Employee, All Open for Manager).

documents.t: Concept What It Does Where Implemented Private Node Local server instance. Routes browser endpoint's server calls to your VS Code for live debugging. Procify Workspace Hub → Endpoints → Node ID Entity .ts file TypeScript class that extends KloEntity. The ONLY place for business logic. workspace/apps/<app>/d_complaints.ts onAfterCreate() Server-side hook — fires after every new record is created. Used for auto-setting defaults. d_complaints.ts OnValidate() Server-side hook — fires on navigation when TransNode setActiveIf = Valid. Blocks save on error. d_complaints.ts + Page Builder TransNode onDelete() Server-side hook — fires after a record is deleted. Used for cascade cleanup. d_complaints.ts Setter (set property) Interceptor for property writes. Computes derived fields. Must call this.s() to persist. d_complaints.ts Getter (get property) Interceptor for property reads. Returns computed/formatted value. Used with transient properties. d_complaints.ts ValidationError Error object pushed to this.errors array. ErrorType.ERROR blocks. WARNING allows with message. OnValidate in d_complaints.ts this.txn KloTransaction — server context. Provides getUserID(), hasPermission(), hasCRUDPermisson(). Inside any entity hook or rule onPageModelReady Controller hook that fires before data is fetched. Best for applying default search filters. p_complaints.controller.ts beforeQ (Query Rule) Server-side hook — fires before a query hits the database. Used for row-level, role-based filtering. q_complaints.ts afterQ (Query Rule) Server-side hook — fires after results return from the database. Used to reshape/compute values across the result set via getResults()/setResults(). . q_complaints.ts Team Group (User Group) Bundle of users assigned in one action to an App Collection, instead of assigning users one at a time. Workspace Hub → Team Groups

documents.t: Reference: Private Node setup Guide The Private Node is a local Node.js server running on your laptop that acts as the workspace server for your development session. Instead of your browser talking to the shared landscape server, it talks to your VS Code instance — giving you full debugging capability and instant iteration on server-side code.

documents.t: The entity .ts file for d_complaints is located in the Private Node workspace at the path: workspace/apps/<your_app_id>/d_complaints.ts If the file does not exist yet, the private node can generate it. The base structure looks like this: import { KloEntity, ValidationError, ErrorType } from 'klobase'; export class d_complaints extends KloEntity { // ── Getters & Setters ────────────────────────────────────────── // ── Lifecycle Hooks ──────────────────────────────────────────── public async onAfterCreate(): Promise<any> { // Called after a new complaint record is created } public async OnValidate(): Promise<any> { // Called during navigation if transnode setActiveIf = Valid } public async onDelete(): Promise<any> { // Called after the record is deleted } } 💡 Architecture Principle: Business Logic Belongs Here The entity file is the authoritative location for all business logic. Period. Controller file → UI orchestration only (navigation, formatter functions, show/hide decisions). Entity file → field defaults, cross-field computations, validations, role enforcement. Never duplicate validation logic in the controller. If the controller calls commitP(), OnValidate() fires automatically on the server — that is your safety net. Reference: kloTouch 7.0 Basic Training Guide — Section 7.5 Best Practice Do's and Don'ts (Entity File).
documents.s: A.2 — Entity File Location and Structure
documents.u: /Procify_Documentation/docs/Docs/Training Guide/Beginner Training Guide/Session 5 — BOL Logic & Validations/Part A — Setting Up the Private Node Environment

documents.t: Klobase provides three entity lifecycle hook methods that you override in the entity .ts file. These run on the server and are triggered automatically by the platform at the appropriate point in the entity's lifecycle. Method When Called Trigger Condition Primary Use onAfterCreate() After entity is created in DB On every new entity save Set defaults, auto-populate audit fields, initialise related records OnValidate() During navigation / on save / validateP function TransNode setActiveIf = 'Valid' Validate field values, enforce business rules, push errors onDelete() After entity is deleted On every delete operation Cascade cleanup, logging, send notifications 📘 OnValidate — Important Details OnValidate is triggered ONLY when the TransNode's 'setActiveIf' property is set to 'Valid' in the Page Builder. If setActiveIf is not set, OnValidate does NOT fire — the platform skips validation on navigation. Inside OnValidate, push errors using: this.errors.push(new ValidationError(this, propertyId, errorCode, message, ErrorType.ERROR)); The method must NOT return the errors array — it pushes to this.errors and the platform reads it. (PROC-24075 fixed this for proper return type.) ErrorType.ERROR blocks save. ErrorType.WARNING allows save but shows a warning toast. After your OnValidate runs, the platform ALSO runs its own mandatory-field validation based on key attributes — you don't need to repeat those.

documents.t: Rules contain business logic codes. It works with the event bus, any change in the entity will trigger the event, and all the rules hooked with the event will be executed sequentially. Rules are reusable objects across client, server and middleware. EX: When a complaint is created by an employee then status should be OPEN and assigned_to should be the same user. A responsible team/manager/assigned_to can be assigned by the manager only. An employee or manager can delete the complaint but not the responsible team Field Default Value Logic s_status 'OPEN' — every new complaint starts in OPEN status assigned_to this.txn.getUserID() — auto-set to the logged-in user who created the complaint created_on this.s_created_on — already auto-set by system field, no action needed created_by this.s_created_by — already auto-set by system field, no action needed

documents.t: Step 1: Go to the Rule tab and click on the add icon(+). Field Description Event type Select the event type. Based on the type of event you choose, the rule will be executed. Type Select the channel type, based on this the transaction will be performed. Exit ID is an ID you put in for the rule subscription. (can select from the existing one). Clazz This will be the rule file name. Invocation Method The method needs to be called. Step 2: Select the Event Type from the drop-down. The event type will mention when the rules will be executed. Event types: On Create ( rule will be executed on create of an entity) On Delete (rule will be executed on delete of an entity) On Update (rule will be executed on update of an entity) Rest of the types will be covered in future. Step 3: Select the channel type(there are different input channels to perform a transaction on an entity, channel type selection decides when to trigger the Rule). Channel Type: Endpoint / Device on Klarion server- always on the client Endpoint / Device on Klarion server Endpoint / Device on Klarion server- always on server(current focus) Endpoint / Device to Server/ Client -Network Context Switch Legacy on Klarion server Klarion server to Klarion offline server Klarion server to Klarion Server Step 4: Fill in the value for Exit ID. Exit ID: It's an ID that you put in for the rule subscription. (can select from the existing one). Step 5: In the Clazz field provide the rule file name (example: rules/<file_name>) and in the invocation method provide an event name. You will be using that event to write your business logic codes. NOTE: If you are creating a Rule for the same entity you can fill this inside the Clazz field. Step 6: Click on the save button to save the newly created rule.

documents.t: TypeScript property accessors let you intercept reads and writes of entity properties. In Klobase, setters and getters in the entity .ts file are the correct place for computed/derived field logic — not the controller. Pattern Purpose Setter (set propertyId) Called every time the property value changes. Use to: compute a derived field when an input changes, enforce value formatting, trigger side-effects. Getter (get propertyId) Called every time the property value is read. Use to: return a computed / formatted value instead of the raw stored value. ⚠ Critical Setter Pattern — Always Call this.s() Inside a setter, you MUST call this.s('propertyId', new_value, 'dataType', false, false) to actually persist the new value into the entity's internal state. Without this.s(), the new_value is accepted by TypeScript but never written to the entity data — the save will ignore your change. Pattern: if(new_value == this.propertyId) return; // guard to avoid infinite loop Then: this.s('propertyId', new_value, 'dataType', false, false);
documents.s: D.1 — What Are Setters and Getters?
documents.u: /Procify_Documentation/docs/Docs/Training Guide/Beginner Training Guide/Session 5 — BOL Logic & Validations/Part D — Property Setters and Getters

documents.t: When a complaint is closed (closed_on is set), actual_tat should be computed as: (closed_on - created_on) in days. public set closed_on(new_value: Date) { if (new_value == this.closed_on) return; this.s('closed_on', new_value, 'date', false, false); // Compute actual_tat when closed_on is set if (new_value && this.s_created_on) { const msPerDay = 1000 * 60 * 60 * 24; const diffMs = new Date(new_value).getTime() - new Date(this.s_created_on).getTime(); this.actual_tat = parseFloat((diffMs / msPerDay).toFixed(1)); } }

documents.t: A getter can return a formatted composite string. For example, a display_title getter that combines complaint_id and priority: // t_ prefix = transient property (not stored in DB) // Define t_display_title as a Transient property in the Procify Data Studio first public get t_display_title(): string { return ${this.complaint_id} [${this.priority || 'UNSET'}]; } 📘 Transient Properties (Procify Data Studio 7.0 User Guide — Entity Property Qualifier) Transient properties (t_ prefix) are computed at runtime and NOT stored in the database. They must still be defined as entity properties in the Procify Data Studio with qualifier = Transient. Once defined, they can be added to sections and controls in the Page Builder like any other property. The getter in the .ts file provides the value — the platform reads the getter whenever the control renders. Use transient properties for: display labels, formatted dates, computed totals, role-based display logic.

documents.t: Based on the BRD from Session 1, the following validations must be enforced when a complaint is saved: Rule ID Field(s) Condition Message V001 complaint_desc Empty or length < 10 chars Complaint description must be at least 10 characters. V002 priority Empty (null or blank) Priority is required. Please select Low / Medium / High / Critical. V003 planned_resolution_date Set AND is before today's date The planned resolution date cannot be in the past. V004 planned_resolution_date Set AND is before created_on The planned resolution date cannot be before the complaint creation date. V005 s_status Attempt to set CLOSED but role is Employee Employees cannot close a complaint. Only the manager can close.
documents.s: E.1 — Validation Rules for the Customer Complaints App

documents.t: public async OnValidate(): Promise<any> { // V001 — complaint_desc minimum length if (!this.complaint_desc || this.complaint_desc.trim().length < 10) { this.errors.push(new ValidationError( this, 'complaint_desc', 'V001', 'Complaint description must be at least 10 characters.', ErrorType.ERROR )); } // V002 — priority is required if (!this.priority) { this.errors.push(new ValidationError( this, 'priority', 'V002', 'Priority is required.', ErrorType.ERROR )); } // V003 — planned_resolution_date not in the past if (this.planned_resolution_date) { const today = new Date(); today.setHours(0, 0, 0, 0); if (new Date(this.planned_resolution_date) < today) { this.errors.push(new ValidationError( this, 'planned_resolution_date', 'V003', 'Planned resolution date cannot be in the past.', ErrorType.ERROR )); } } // V004 — planned_resolution_date not before created_on if (this.planned_resolution_date && this.s_created_on) { if (new Date(this.planned_resolution_date) < new Date(this.s_created_on)) { this.errors.push(new ValidationError( this, 'planned_resolution_date', 'V004', 'Planned resolution date cannot be before the complaint creation date.', ErrorType.ERROR )); } } } 📘 Role Rollup Values (Training Guide Beginner — Session 1 Part A) s_role_rollup is the numeric role hierarchy value assigned to application roles. Owner (Employee role) → s_role_rollup = 10 Supervisor (Manager role) → s_role_rollup = 20 Reviewer (ResponsibleTeam role) → s_role_rollup = 30 Lower number = higher priority. Manager (20) overrides Employee (10). You can also use this.txn.hasPermission('permission_id') for custom permission checks. See Permissions User Guide.

documents.t: # Action Detail / Code 1 Save d_complaints.ts Save the file. Private Node restarts automatically. 2 Test V001 — short description In the UI, open a complaint detail. Clear the complaint_desc field or enter only 3 characters. Click Save. The platform should block navigation and highlight complaint_desc with the error message 'Complaint description must be at least 10 characters'. 3 Test V002 — missing priority Clear the priority field. Click Save. Priority field should be highlighted with the V002 error message. 4 Test V003 — past date Set planned_resolution_date to yesterday. Click Save. Should show V003 error on the date field. 5 Test V005 — Employee closing complaint Log in as emp_<prid> (Employee role). Open a complaint. Change s_status to CLOSED. Try to Save. Should see V005 error. Log in as mgr_<prid> (Manager) — same operation should succeed. 6 Verify valid record saves Fill all required fields correctly with a future resolution date. Click Save. Record should commit without errors. Check Private Node terminal — no error logs. Part E — Query Rules E.1 — What are Query Rules? ` around a create/update/delete. They are the correct place to answer two very different questions: Before the database is asked anything — “what should this user even be allowed to see?” (row-level filtering, defaulting search criteria). After the database has answered — “does the raw result need reshaping before it reaches the client?” (adding computed fields, merging data from a second query, masking sensitive values, sorting/aggregating in ways the query modeller can’t express. Both callbacks receive an EventContext (commonly named oEvent) and give access to the query instance itself via oEvent.getObject(). E.1 — How to Create Query Rules? Creating query rules is the same as creating entity rules, except the event type you subscribe to is one of: Event types: Before Query (beforeQ) — executes before the query is fired against the database. Anything set on the query object here becomes part of the WHERE condition. After Query (afterQ) — executes after results come back from the database, before they are returned to the client. The raw result set can be read and replaced here. Query Rule Event Reference (BOL API) Event.getObject() — returns the KloQueryForRule instance being executed. Set properties on it to add filter conditions (beforeQ), or call getResults() / setResults() on it to read/replace the raw result rows (afterQ). Event.getTxn() — returns the KloTransaction for the current user; use it to read $SYSTEM.roleID, call this.txn.get$User(), or check permissions. Event.getEventType() — returns which event fired, e.g. BEFORE_QUERY or AFTER_QUERY. Useful if one method is wired to handle both events. queryInstance.getResults() / setResults() — read or replace the raw JSON array of result rows in an afterQ callback. These are plain objects, not KloEntity instances — they cannot be saved back.

documents.t: As we already know from the BRD document complaints page behaviour will be different based on role. In case of employee only complaints raised by him should be visible In case of manager all the complaints should be visible In case of it_team only assigned tickets should be visible Create query folder and q_complaints.ts public async beforeQ(oEvent: EventContext) { let obj : any = oEvent.getObject(); let role = oEvent.getTxn().$SYSTEM.roleID; if(role === 'EMPLOYEE'){ obj.customer_id = (await this.txn.get$User()).login_id; obj.s_created_by = (await this.txn.get$User()).login_id; // Added for Business AI }else if( role == "IT_TEAM"){ obj.assigned_to = (await this.txn.get$User()).login_id; } if(obj.description) { obj.description = `%${obj.description}%`; } }

documents.t: The Manager’s complaint list needs a column showing how many days a complaint has been open — days_open — without storing it on the entity (it changes every day, so persisting it would immediately go stale). documents.t: public async afterQ(oEvent: EventContext) { let queryInstance = oEvent.getObject(); let results = await queryInstance.getResults(); let today = new Date(); let newResults = results.map((row: any) => { if (row.s_created_on) { let created = new Date(row.s_created_on); let diffMs = today.getTime() - created.getTime(); row.days_open = Math.floor(diffMs / (1000 * 60 * 60 * 24)); } else { row.days_open = 0; } return row; }); queryInstance.setResults(newResults); }
